overview_intro: A summary of your situation based on what you shared — so we start from the same place.
overview_value_worry: “I don’t know where to start with all the paperwork.”
overview_note_text: I've read through everything you shared and I have a clear picture of your situation. The paperwork anxiety is completely normal — and it's exactly why I've structured this guide around your specific timeline and priorities. Start with Section 2 and follow the order. I'm here if anything comes up.
before_intro: Things to sort while still in your home country — documents to gather, accounts to notify, and things to close or suspend before departure. Tick each item as you complete it.
before_item1_text: Passport — valid for at least 6 months beyond your intended stay. Bring originals + certified photocopies. Store digital copies in Google Drive or iCloud.
before_item2_text: Birth certificate — with apostille and certified English translation. Required for banking, and official processes. Get this done before you leave.
before_item3_text: Marriage certificate (if applicable) — apostille + certified English translation. Required for joint banking, and US administrative processes.
before_item4_text: Home country driving licence — original. You need this to apply for your US state licence. Keep it safe.
before_item5_text: Medical records & vaccination history — get copies from your Italian doctor (medico di base). US providers will ask for these. Note: some Italian vaccines differ from the US schedule.
before_item6_text: Prescription medications — 3+ months supply + a doctor's letter explaining your treatment in English. You cannot use an Italian prescription (ricetta), pharmacies will require a US prescription.
before_item7_text: Financial documents — last 3 years of tax returns (dichiarazioni dei redditi), recent bank statements, proof of savings. May be required by US landlords and some banks.
banking_intro:
Two things define your financial life in the US from day one: your bank account and your credit score.
In Italy, your ability to rent or borrow is based on income and employment. In the US, it's based on your credit score — and you're starting from zero.
banking_account_intro: Opening a US bank account — you can open a basic account before you have an SSN, but you will need a US address first. Most banks require an in-person visit for non-residents.
banking_step1_title: What most US banks require from new immigrants
banking_step1_desc:
• Valid passport (primary ID)
• Proof of US address (lease agreement, utility bill, or official letter with your name and US address)
• SSN or ITIN — some banks allow opening without one initially, but features will be limited
banking_step2_title: Bridge solution before a full account
banking_step2_desc:
Wise allows you to hold USD and make transfers without a US bank account — useful for the first weeks while you set up a proper account.
It is not a US bank account but works for day-to-day spending and EUR→USD transfers at much better rates than your home bank's international wire.
banking_step3_title: Once SSN arrives — update your bank account
banking_step3_desc: Go to your branch and add your SSN to unlock full account features: higher transfer limits, credit card eligibility, and better account types.
healthcare_intro: This is the section that shocks every Italian moving to the US. You're coming from a country where healthcare is a constitutional right, funded by taxes, free at point of use. The US system works entirely differently.
healthcare_row1_italy: Universal public healthcare. Funded by taxes. Free or very low cost at point of use for all residents.
healthcare_row1_us: Mixed private/public. Most people get insurance through employer or buy privately. No universal coverage.
healthcare_row2_italy: Free with your primary care physician. Specialists require prescriptions + small ticket.
healthcare_row2_us: Copay per visit ($20–50+). Must use in-network doctors or costs are much higher.
healthcare_row3_italy: Heavily subsidised. Most medications cost €1–5 with SSN.
healthcare_row3_us: Vary widely — $10 to $300+/month depending on plan and medication.
healthcare_row4_us: Covered but you pay deductible. An ER visit can cost $500–$5,000+ even with insurance.
healthcare_row5_italy: Partially covered for emergencies. Most routine dental is private.
healthcare_row5_us: Completely separate dental insurance. Routine care (cleanings, fillings) not covered by standard health plans.
healthcare_row6_us: Average employer plan: $400–800/month in premiums (employer pays most). Plus deductible + copays.
healthcare_warning_text: A single night in a US hospital without insurance: $10,000–50,000. A broken arm: $3,000–7,000. An ER visit: $1,500–5,000. Until US insurance is active, maintain at minimum a travel insurance policy covering medical emergencies.
housing_intro: How US renting works — and what's different from Italy. Personalised to your city, your budget, and what you told me.
housing_row1_italy: Usually 4+4 or 3+2 years. Cancellation with notice period.
housing_row1_us: Usually 12-month lease. Month-to-month possible but more expensive. 30-60 days notice to leave.
housing_row2_italy: Employment contract, income. Credit rarely checked.
housing_row2_us: Credit score (620+ typical), income (3x monthly rent), references, background check.
housing_row3_us: Usually 1–2 months. Higher if no credit history.
housing_row4_us: Usually no agency fee for renters — landlord pays the broker.
housing_row5_us: Most rentals are unfurnished — no appliances, curtains, or light fixtures included.
housing_row6_us: Almost always separate. You pay electricity, gas, water, internet yourself.
housing_row7_us: Buildings are explicitly pet-friendly or not. Pet deposit usually required ($200–500).
driving_intro: Getting your driving licence in the US is one of the most important early steps — in most American cities, including Minneapolis, a car is essential for daily life. The process differs by state.
daily_intro: The small things nobody warns you about — the culture shocks, the practical differences, the things that make you feel lost in a supermarket at 9pm.
community_intro: This is the section nobody talks about enough. The paperwork is hard, but the loneliness is harder. Building a life from scratch takes time — and that's completely normal.
checklist_intro: Every action from this guide in one place, ordered by timeline. Tick items off as you go.
timeline_intro: A clean, ordered roadmap of what to do and when. Each item links to the deep-dive section for full details. Don't try to do everything at once — follow this sequence.
timeline_block1_task1:
Phone — you can keep using your home country number with an international plan or roaming, or get a US eSIM alongside your existing SIM.
T-Mobile and AT&T are the most widely available carriers. A US phone number is useful for bank verification texts and local services.
timeline_block1_task2: Essentials — locate your nearest grocery store, pharmacy, and urgent care clinic — find these before you need them.
timeline_block1_task3: Finances — transfer initial funds from your Italian bank via Wise — better rates than a bank wire.
timeline_block1_task4: Short-term housing should be arranged before you arrive — Airbnb, extended-stay hotel, or furnished short-term rental.
timeline_block2_task1: Apply for your SSN — this is your priority, your bank account and everything else depends on it.
timeline_block2_task2: Open a US bank account — Chase, Bank of America, or Sable are the best options for newcomers.
timeline_block2_task3: Long-term apartment — start visiting the apartments, booking visits before landing. Don't rush into the first option, but don't delay the search.
timeline_block2_task4: Driving licence process — download and study your state's Driver's Manual, book the knowledge test.
